title: Deep Research Agents and Landscape Scans
answer: Deep research agents and landscape scans cover the use of autonomous or semi-autonomous software to plan, run and report on broad literature searches. A landscape scan maps a field by identifying key papers, methods, models, tools, datasets and open questions, often before a formal systematic review is attempted. Deep research agents extend this by breaking a research question into sub-questions, retrieving sources, extracting claims and assembling a structured summary. The scope is evidence synthesis, not primary data collection, and it includes scoping reviews, rapid reviews and horizon scanning.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Deep research agents and landscape scans cover the use of autonomous or semi-autonomous software to plan, run and report on broad literature searches. A landscape scan maps a field by identifying key papers, methods, models, tools, datasets and open questions, often before a formal systematic review is attempted. Deep research agents extend this by breaking a research question into sub-questions, retrieving sources, extracting claims and assembling a structured summary. On this site the library holds 135 research papers and 12993 claims extracted from research works, which shows the scale of evidence a scan can be expected to handle. The scope is evidence synthesis, not primary data collection, and it includes scoping reviews, rapid reviews and horizon scanning.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on large language models combined with retrieval layers, document parsers, embedding stores and orchestration code that manages multi-step tasks. They depend on access to scholarly databases, publisher APIs, open access repositories, web search and local file stores, plus compute and storage for indexing and reranking. A landscape scan also needs a structured catalogue of entities, and this site provides 91 AI books, 798 scientific models, 732 AI tools and 686 glossary terms as reference points. Logging, versioning and citation capture are part of the infrastructure because every extracted claim must remain traceable. The stack is usually assembled from general purpose components rather than a single product.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a question or a field boundary, then agents generate search queries, retrieve candidate documents and screen them against inclusion criteria. Relevant sources are parsed, claims are extracted, and the claims are coded into a taxonomy of methods, findings, limitations and gaps. Human reviewers check samples, resolve disagreements and validate the final synthesis, because agents can miss context or overstate a finding. Landscape scans often use tables or maps to show coverage across subfields, and they record where evidence is thin. The output is a draft synthesis with links to the original papers, not a finished review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on copyright, database terms, attribution and the handling of personal or sensitive data. Provenance is the main safeguard, and the working rule is that every claim points to the original paper rather than to a search tool or a secondary summary. This site never links to the Consensus search tool, and it links to the original paper instead, which keeps the chain of evidence clear. Risks include fabricated citations, misattributed claims, paywall violations, biased retrieval and over-reliance on agent output without expert review. Common practice is to document prompts, model versions, retrieval dates and inclusion decisions so that a scan can be audited or reproduced.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more capable agents that can run longer searches, handle tables and figures, and maintain living landscape scans that update as new papers appear. Evaluation is becoming a central concern, with benchmarks for citation accuracy, coverage, recall and resistance to fabricated sources. Integration with systematic review software and structured reporting standards is likely to grow, as is the use of provenance graphs that link each claim to its source. Multilingual and multimodal scanning will expand the evidence base beyond English text. The human role is shifting toward framing questions, setting inclusion criteria and auditing the agent's trail.
